lead.t: Chest wall & diaphragm mechanics – rib cage, intercostals, diaphragm: Restriction from stiff lungs limits tidal volume; the diaphragm must generate higher pressures, which is why patients develop rapid, shallow breathing and early fatigue.

snip.t: Chest wall & diaphragm mechanics – rib cage, intercostals, diaphragm: Restriction from stiff lungs limits tidal volume; the diaphragm must generate higher pressures, which is why patients develop rapid, shallow breathing and early fatigue.
The liver is the second largest organ, weighing about three pounds, located under the right rib cage.
BMI & waist circumference: Measure weight, height, waist at midpoint between iliac crest and rib cage — BMI quantifies overall adiposity; waist >94 cm (men) or >80 cm (women) signals visceral fat.
Reduced chest expansion – “shiny” skin over thorax, decreased inspiratory depth: Skin and sub‑cutaneous fibrosis restrict rib cage movement, predisposing to restrictive lung pattern.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The rib cage is a bony framework of 12 pairs of ribs, the sternum, and thoracic vertebrae that protects vital thoracic organs and assists breathing. Its shape and integrity are essential for ventilation and trauma assessment.

sections.p: The rib cage forms a semi‑rigid barrel surrounding the heart, lungs, and great vessels, providing protection and a lever for respiratory muscles.
Ribs articulate posteriorly with thoracic vertebrae and anteriorly with the sternum (via costal cartilages) forming a flexible yet sturdy enclosure.
b: True ribs (1‑7) directly attach to sternum
False ribs (8‑12) attach via cartilage; 11‑12 are floating

sections.p: Anteriorly the rib cage overlies the liver (right), spleen (left), and diaphragm; posteriorly it contacts the spinal column and paravertebral muscles.
Intercostal arteries (branches of the aorta) run along the inferior border of each rib, supplying bone, muscle, and overlying skin.
Intercostal nerves (T1‑T11) run with the vessels in the neurovascular bundle, providing sensory innervation to the thoracic wall and motor to intercostals.
Provides rigid protection for thoracic viscera, serves as attachment for respiratory muscles, and expands/ contracts during inspiration and expiration.
Rib fractures, flail chest, and costochondritis are common; they can compromise ventilation, cause underlying organ injury, or mimic cardiac pain.
b: Rib fracture: pain, impaired breathing, risk of pneumothorax
Flail chest: paradoxical movement, respiratory failure
Costochondritis: chest wall tenderness, non‑cardiac pain

t.b: Detects rib fractures, pneumothorax, hemothorax; if unavailable, use bedside ultrasound or clinical assessment
Defines complex fractures, mediastinal injury; if unavailable, rely on X‑ray + physical exam

sections.p: Inspection, palpation of each rib, and auscultation for breath sounds are key. Note any deformity, tenderness, or paradoxical motion.
b: Palpate from spine outward to locate fracture site
Listen for diminished breath sounds indicating pneumothorax
Assess respiratory effort for flail segment

whenToSeekHelp: Severe chest pain with dyspnea suggesting pneumothorax or hemothorax
Signs of shock after trauma (hypotension, tachycardia)

faq.q: Why do rib fractures cause shallow breathing?
faq.a: Pain limits deep inspiration, reducing tidal volume and risking atelectasis.

faq.q: How does flail chest affect ventilation?
faq.a: The free segment moves inward on inspiration, impairing lung expansion and causing respiratory failure.

faq.q: Can costochondritis be confused with heart attack?
faq.a: Yes; both cause chest pain, but costochondritis is reproducible on palpation and lacks ECG changes.

exam: Describe the anatomical differences between true, false, and floating ribs.
Explain how a rib fracture can lead to a pneumothorax and what clinical signs you would look for.
Identify the neurovascular bundle location on a rib and its clinical significance.
